title: Rowan and the Lost Mouse
markdown:
Once upon a time, nestled high in the cloudy hills where soft clouds often brushed the mountaintops like gentle wool, lived a young witch named Rowan. Her cottage was snug and round, with a little chimney that always puffed out sweet-smelling smoke. It smelled like honey and warm embers from the hearth.

Every day Rowan’s world was warm and lovely, filled with the gentle rhythm of learning. She would wake with the first shy light of dawn, her soft lavender cloak settling around her shoulders. Then she would practice making little stones float and swirl gently in the air, like playful little lights. After that she would carefully collect shiny moonbeams in tiny glass jars, which sparkled like captured starlight, perfect for lighting her small workspace.

One day, while she was gently gathering soft herbs near a mossy stone that hummed with quiet magic, Rowan heard a tiny worried squeak. It was a sound so small it was almost lost in the rustling leaves. Peeking under a big green fern leaf, its fronds opening like sleepy green hands, she found a very small mouse. Its fur was the soft warm colour of a fallen leaf after a gentle rain. Its whiskers twitched with a whisper of worry, trembling ever so slightly.

Rowan’s heart felt a little flutter, softer than a dandelion’s fluff on the breeze. She knew this little mouse was not just exploring. He was lost, and perhaps a little lonely.

Hand in tiny paw, we’ll find your home.

A gentle worry settled in her tummy, like a little cloud wanting to float away. She knew, with a certainty as warm as her hearth fire, that she must help this little creature find his way home before the last light of the sun faded from the sky.

“Don’t worry, little one,” she whispered, her voice as soft as falling snow. “We’ll find your home together. Just you wait and see.”

She carefully scooped the mouse onto her open hand. His tiny paws, no bigger than rose petals, felt like silken threads against her skin. The mouse, whom Rowan decided to call Pipkin because his tiny nose seemed to wiggle so much, squeaked a little, a sound like a very tiny faraway bell. He snuggled into her warm palm, feeling safe.

Rowan and Pipkin began a quiet journey through the whispering woods. They tiptoed past the tall whispering pines, their needles murmuring secrets to the breeze. The path ahead was dappled with the soft silvery light of the afternoon sun filtering through the leaves. Pipkin, feeling a little braver with Rowan’s gentle warmth, pointed his delicate nose toward a faint winding path that led deeper into the shelter of the trees. They walked and walked, the only sounds their soft footsteps on the mossy ground and Pipkin’s occasional tiny sighs of hopeful expectation.

Hand in tiny paw, we’ll find your home.

As they ambled along, their journey led them to a funny little hut nestled in a sunlit clearing. The hut seemed to be overflowing with scrolls and maps. They spilled out of the door like a gentle waterfall of old paper, rustling softly in the breeze. Standing outside, peering intently at a map the size of a small tablecloth, was an old wizard with a long snowy beard that tickled his knees and a kindly twinkle in his bright blue eyes. This was Wizard Abernathy, known far and wide for having rather a lot of maps for every single thing you could imagine.

Rowan approached him, Pipkin still nestled safely in her hand, his little nose occasionally nudging her thumb. “Excuse me, wise Wizard Abernathy,” she began politely. “I’m trying to help this little mouse find his burrow. Do you happen to have a map of tiny mouse homes anywhere?”

Wizard Abernathy blinked, then let out a chuckle like dry leaves rustling on a pathway. “A map of mouse homes, you say? Well, I do believe I have a map of just about everything else under the sun. Let’s have a look, shall we?”

He unfurled another scroll, and then another, until maps were piled all around them, creating a colourful papery landscape. Rowan waited patiently. Then Pipkin suddenly wriggled in her hand, pointing his tiny nose with great excitement toward a very old faded map that showed the base of a particularly knobbly oak tree, marked with a tiny dotted line.

“That one!” he squeaked, a little louder this time, full of newfound confidence.

Rowan felt a rush of warm happiness bloom in her chest. She looked up at Wizard Abernathy, who was now happily trying to fold a map that clearly did not want to be folded, its edges curling up playfully.

“Thank you ever so much, Wizard Abernathy! We found it thanks to your wonderful maps!”

The wizard waved a distracted but cheerful hand, happily buried in his map mountain. Rowan and Pipkin hurried toward the knobbly oak tree. And there, nestled among its sturdy roots, almost hidden by soft green moss, was a cozy little opening, its entrance lined with the softest warmest moss. Pipkin gave a joyful triumphant squeak and scurried happily into his home. He peeked out, his worried whiskers now replaced with happy enthusiastic wiggles.

As the moon climbed higher in the velvety night sky, painting the cloudy hills in pearl and gentle lavender, Rowan sat on a soft patch of moss near Pipkin’s burrow. She watched the fireflies begin to blink, like tiny waltzing stars on the ground. She listened to the quiet night—the soft hoot of a distant owl, the gentle sigh of the wind, the chirping of crickets. Pipkin, tucked snugly in his mossy bed, began to dream.

Rowan walked back to her cozy cottage under a million stars, a pleasant wave of sleepiness washing over her. The jars of moonbeams were still on the table, waiting for morning practice. The fern leaf, back in the woods, had closed its sleepy green hands.

Hand in tiny paw, they had found his home.
characters: Rowan (young witch of the cloudy hills), Pipkin (lost leaf-coloured mouse)
author: StoryGen Community
